sentences.text: Rahonavis was a small predator measuring about 70 cm in length and weighing between 0.45 and 2.27 kg.
The name Rahonavis means "cloud menace bird," derived from the Malagasy words for cloud or menace combined with the Latin word for bird.
The only known specimen of Rahonavis, a partial skeleton cataloged as UA 8656, was discovered by Catherine Forster and colleagues.
Fossils were first recovered in 1995 by a joint expedition from SUNY and the University of Antananarivo near the village of Berivotra, Madagascar.
The discoverers originally named the genus Rahona but renamed it Rahonavis after finding that Rahona was already used for a genus of moths.

Despite artistic depictions showing flight, it is unclear if Rahonavis could fly, and some doubt exists regarding whether the forearm material with quill knobs belongs to the same skeleton as the rest of the remains.
Luis M. Chiappe argued that Rahonavis could probably fly, citing its large, robust ulna and prominent quill knobs as evidence of larger and more powerful wings than those of Archaeopteryx.
Agnolín and Novas (2013) suggested that, similar to Microraptor, Rahonavis likely used a bat-like flight stroke utilizing the deltoideus muscle complexes.
There has been historical uncertainty regarding whether Rahonavis belongs to the bird clade Avialae or is a closely related dromaeosaurid.
Rahonavis belongs to the parent group Unenlagiinae and is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae.
Rahonavis is classified as a reptile.
Rahonavis lived in northwestern Madagascar during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago.
Rahonavis lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
As of 2020, paleontologists remain undecided whether Rahonavis is an unenlagiine, a dromaeosaurid, or an avialan.
